title: Greg Mazares Sr. on AI, E-Discovery, and the Future of Human-Led Legal Services
author: Greg Mazares Sr.

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Mazares accepts the cluster’s core forecast that AI will compress billable production without eliminating hourly billing and that junior development must be redesigned rather than abandoned. He materially extends it by proposing a specific successor role for juniors: AI advisers who combine legal grounding with technology expertise and may teach senior partners and clients. His claims are qualified professional predictions, not measured evidence.
qs: So I think what’s going to happen is they will bill hours, but they will probably bill hours for different levels of services at lower levels of hours, but at higher rates in some cases, in many cases.

I think they’re now going to have to not only get a grounding in the law, obviously,  but they’re going to have to now elevate to becoming experts in the use and application of new technology so that they can better help their clients.

st.an: Mazares accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI will compress production hours rather than eliminate lawyers, and concretely extends it by predicting that junior associates will shift toward technology-enabled, higher-value client consulting while firms preserve the experiential training lost as document review declines.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source accepts the need for disciplined AI selection and materially develops it through concrete readiness assessments, workflow sprints, value-based renewal reviews and follow-on procurement support. It also interprets this work as movement away from FOMO-driven purchasing, although the evidence is advisory experience rather than quantified market-wide outcomes.
qs: And they’ll engage us to run a similar kind of sprint format with a different discovery focus, and we’ll help them surface where that existing tool is and isn’t generating value for the business, help the firm understand why that might be,  and then provide them with the kind of objective understanding needed to really inform that go, no-go decision on renewal.

And we’re finding that those AI enablement projects often lead into further work around AI procurement, which I think is a really encouraging sign that the industry is moving beyond the FOMO and the push to buy something now and  figure out how to use it later.

st.an: Mazares supports bounded delegation of routine work while retaining people and effective processes, aligning with the cluster’s emphasis on human involvement and workflow design. The source offers no substantive evidence on multistep reliability, verification bottlenecks or autonomous performance.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Mazares supports the synthesis’s core proposition: automating junior document review risks removing an important source of legal learning, so firms must preserve substantive training while developing juniors’ AI expertise. He also aligns with the anticipated shift toward technology-enabled advisory work and fewer billable hours, though he offers predictions rather than evidence of observed outcomes.
qs: But I think junior associates got so much training from reviewing documents and understanding what the documents contain and the different types of information and issues and so forth.

I think they’re now going to have to not only get a grounding in the law, obviously,  but they’re going to have to now elevate to becoming experts in the use and application of new technology so that they can better help their clients.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Mazares endorses continuous, selective learning through curated alerts, regular reading and trusted professional conversations, while cautioning against complacency and long-range certainty. This aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on practical awareness and contextual filtering rather than chasing every release; his recommendations remain experience-based rather than measured evidence.
qs: Now I’m going to convert my Google Alerts into an AI deliverable because I can get an assessment each day of what’s happening in the industry, et cetera, et cetera.
I think having conversations with people in the industry that we trust is a great way to learn.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Mazares supports the cluster’s implementation thesis that legal AI depends on institutional absorption rather than technology access alone. He emphasizes capable people, disciplined processes, gradual and uneven adoption, and embedded AI expertise, though he does not substantively address pricing pressure, verification or the apprenticeship problem.
qs: But I think the combination of great people working with and implementing impeccable processes using AI, that’s going to be the winning formula for everybody going forward.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Mazares supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI will compress routine associate work and reshape, rather than simply eliminate, junior roles. He also affirms the resulting development challenge: firms must preserve legal learning while adding technology expertise. His claims are forecasts and practitioner judgments, not evidence of realised professional outcomes.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Mazares supports the cluster’s proposition that AI’s benefits depend on organisational and human adaptation. He predicts that junior associates will remain but may be fewer and more capable, while treating productivity gains and flourishing as conditional forecasts rather than measured outcomes.
qs: But I don’t see, there may not  be quite as many junior associates, but those that there are, it’s going to be like having two or three people because they’re going to be able to use amazing personal knowledge coupled with very powerful technology.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that legal AI adoption is an uneven, multiyear organisational change rather than a one-off software deployment. Its strongest alignment is the reported integration of AI specialists into law-firm teams, although it offers little evidence on incentives, connected data or specific workflow redesign.

st.an: Mazares directly supports selective, human-led deployment: AI should automate routine tasks while experienced professionals retain judgment, apply tested workflows and provide layered oversight. kp.k: AI complements people through carefully designed processes
kp.d: Mazares argues that successful legal-services adoption depends on experienced people implementing strong processes, rather than technology alone. He recommends automating simple, repetitive tasks in both client-facing work and internal operations to release time for higher-level client and colleague support. This is his strategic prescription, not a measured productivity finding.
qs: The age of AI is about technology, people, and process.
First and foremost, I think we need to look at are there tasks that are relatively simple and easy and almost machine-like that AI can replace for people?
So it’s not AI or people, it’s AI plus people,

kp.k: Historical automation illustrates redeployment rather than inevitable job elimination
kp.d: Mazares uses a personal recollection from Carnation as an analogy for adapting to AI: an IBM Selectric reduced marketing-department support staffing from six people to one, but the other five were redeployed. He similarly recalls the transition from paper discovery to digital images. These historical anecdotes underpin his optimism about adaptation; they are not evidence of current AI employment outcomes.
qs: And they cut six people down to one person to support the entire marketing department at that point in time.
But the other thing I learned is that the other five people, rather than eliminating them, they were redeployed in other roles.
I see AI as an amazing opportunity,  not a problem.

kp.k: Expert judgment supplies defensibility alongside faster AI workflows
kp.d: Gebauer frames Purpose XI and Case Optics as promising early case insights in days rather than weeks; Mazares responds that experienced specialists add judgment, tested workflows and risk-reducing guardrails. He presents expert involvement as essential to client confidence, but provides neither a quantified speed comparison nor a detailed validation protocol.
qs: And these experts are able to develop workflows that are tested, that are true, that are defensible in nature, that reduce risk.
When I talk about defensibility and we talk about guardrails, we’re talking about  clients who want to use the technology, but want to also know that they’re not going to be criticized.

kp.k: Clients reportedly retain experts rather than fully insourcing AI
kp.d: Mazares reports that some clients initially expected providers to teach them AI and then become unnecessary, but now anticipate continuing relationships because providers supply experience, judgment and defensibility. These are customer views carried by the provider, not independently documented buyer findings. Mazares characterizes adoption as uneven evolution over many years rather than a simultaneous industry-wide revolution.
qs: Now they’re saying, we think it’s going to be a long time, if not forever, that we’re going to need to work with people like you because you add a layer of experience, judgment, and you give us the guardrails and the  defensibility that we need to be even more efficient and effective in the work that we do.
I would call it an evolution rather than a revolution.
it’s not changing all at one time. It’s something that’s going to happen over many years.

kp.k: Provider work shifts toward embedded, higher-level consulting
kp.d: Mazares describes Purpose Legal's AI specialists as increasingly functioning as extensions of law-firm teams. He reports less elementary work and more higher-level consulting, supported by an advisory group addressing specific client needs. He frames this as a need for providers to adapt both services and revenue generation, without supplying financial or workload measurements.
qs: Jeff is actually viewed as an extension of the law firm team.
We’re probably doing less of the more elementary work  that we might have done in the past, and we’re doing some higher level consulting work right now.
we, like everybody  else, have to adapt to providing services and making money in different ways.

kp.k: Staffing acquisition accommodates uneven adoption of AI review
kp.d: Lambert introduces the Hire Counsel acquisition as occurring in early 2026 and bringing over 70,000 vetted attorneys. Mazares explains its rationale as serving document-review projects with extensive, partial or no AI, which he expects to coexist for a few years even as adoption accelerates. The combined provider can undertake technology-heavy projects requiring few people or deploy hundreds of experienced reviewers; this is a flexibility strategy rather than a claim that all review remains labor-intensive.
qs: not all document review projects are going to utilize AI. And so you will have to have people.
You’re going to have AI all in, AI partly in, and no AI.
we can handle projects that involve very few people because the technology can do lots of the work.
we can put hundreds of people onto a single project who are all experienced, vetted,

kp.k: Growth strategy emphasizes productivity and expertise over data hosting
kp.d: Mazares corrects the host's aggressive-M&A framing, saying most recent growth was organic and acquisitions were selective. He links future growth to making existing people more productive through AI and training. As platforms and law firms increasingly handle hosting themselves, he identifies consulting, forensics, analytics, difficult data problems and progressively larger repeat-client engagements as sources of provider value and profit.
qs: most of it has been organic growth. We haven’t purchased a lot of companies.
Our growth is about the people that we have becoming more and more productive.
Because we’re not just hosting terabytes and terabytes of data anymore.
we’re building the business through repeat clients who start off giving us smaller projects to midsize projects to mega projects to managed services agreements.

kp.k: Cloud discovery requires substantial security investment and shared protection
kp.d: Mazares describes discovery data moving from on-premise infrastructure into cloud environments or clients' own instances. He says Purpose Legal works with platform organizations and invests in an around-the-clock technology team, including employees inside and outside the US, to protect data. These are provider assurances about arrangements and investment, not independently verified security outcomes or a specific account of data-sovereignty controls.
qs: so much of the data, of course, is now stored in the cloud as opposed to on-premise.
We have invested heavily in putting together a large technology group that works around the clock.
Much of the data is also stored on client systems in certain cases where clients have invested in their own instances for data storage.

kp.k: Reviewer conduct creates risks beyond infrastructure security
kp.d: Asked about misplaced security concerns, Mazares says clients can be overly concerned about breaches of reviewed data while underappreciating risks from people and recording technologies. He recounts an incident he heard about elsewhere involving reviewers using '3D glasses' to capture data, describes restrictions on items brought into on-site reviews, and stresses multilayer reviewer vetting. The incident is explicitly hearsay outside his company; he also acknowledges technology can fail.
qs: This wasn’t within our company, but it’s something I’ve heard within the industry.
there’s greater risk because there are a lot of people that you don’t have direct control over
Well, I think you can always have technology failure.
you need to make sure that you vet reviewers properly. You need to have multiple layers of vetting.

kp.k: Junior lawyers may become AI teachers and consultants
kp.d: In response to a three-to-five-year outlook question, Mazares predicts junior associates will become AI ambassadors, advising clients and teaching senior partners how to use new technology. He also identifies a formation problem: document review previously provided substantial exposure to legal information and issues, so juniors must still learn enough law while developing technological expertise. He explicitly qualifies his views by noting that he is not a lawyer.
qs: I think that junior associates are going to become, in my opinion, the ambassadors on how to use AI.
The key thing is to make sure they  still learn enough.
junior associates got so much training from reviewing documents and understanding what the documents contain and the different types of information and issues and so forth.
They may become the teachers to senior partners in some ways.

kp.k: Hourly billing persists with fewer hours and higher rates
kp.d: For the same three-to-five-year horizon, Mazares predicts clients will resist paying for hundreds or thousands of hours when work could take tens of hours. He expects associates to continue billing hourly, but for different services, with fewer hours and higher rates in some or many cases. He anticipates potentially fewer juniors, while suggesting each AI-enabled associate could do the work of two or three people. These are forecasts, not observed billing or headcount results.
qs: clients are not going to want to pay for hundreds and thousands of hours of work that could be done in tens of hours, let’s say.
they will bill hours, but they will probably bill hours for different levels of services at lower levels of hours, but at higher rates in some cases, in many cases.
there may not  be quite as many junior associates
it’s almost like taking one person and turning that one person into two or three that will help carry the day.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mazares predicts augmentation and a shift toward higher-level services, rather than wholesale replacement of legal-service personnel.
pts.d: Greg Mazares argues that AI can replace simple, machine-like tasks, freeing people for higher-level client work. He describes Purpose Legal as already moving from elementary work toward consulting and advisory services. Experienced people, sound processes and technology together—not standalone AI—are his proposed basis for successful service delivery. He also argues that expert-designed workflows add judgment, defensibility and risk reduction. His account of clients wanting continuing expert support is reported customer feedback, not an independently established market-wide finding.

pts.k: Mazares expects mixed levels of AI adoption to sustain demand for both technology-intensive and people-intensive document review.
pts.d: Mazares explains the acquisition of Hire Counsel as a way to serve projects using extensive AI, partial AI or no AI. He anticipates continued demand for experienced reviewers, even while some projects need very few people. He links growth to greater staff productivity and a service mix including consulting, forensics and analytics, rather than data hosting alone. Purpose Legal is discussed as a provider delivering legal support services, not merely a software vendor.

pts.k: Mazares predicts transformed junior-associate roles and fewer billed hours, with higher rates for some services rather than the disappearance of hourly billing.
pts.d: Mazares predicts that juniors will become AI ambassadors, technology specialists and higher-level consultants to clients, potentially teaching senior partners as well. He allows that firms may employ fewer juniors but suggests an AI-enabled individual could perform like two or three people. These are forecasts and illustrative productivity comparisons, not measured staffing or performance results. His pricing forecast retains hourly billing while changing the services billed, reducing hours and raising rates in some or many cases.

pts.k: Sam Moore reports more deliberate AI purchasing and renewal decisions focused on readiness, workflows and demonstrated business value.
pts.d: In the opening advisory segment, Moore describes demand for AI-enablement projects from both first-time purchasers and early adopters approaching renewal. He interprets this as a move beyond fear-driven buying toward more measured procurement. His claim is separate from Mazares's interview and rests on Legal Tech Hub's advisory experience.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on managerial experience, company examples, customer feedback and historical analogy, rather than quantified AI outcome studies.
pts.d: Mazares supports his augmentation argument with a historical example of administrative workers being redeployed after a technology change, and with his account of Purpose Legal's changing work and client relationships. The staffing acquisition illustrates his strategy for heterogeneous demand but does not establish future employment effects. He supplies no measured AI productivity, defensibility, error-rate, staffing or pricing results. Moore similarly offers observations from advisory engagements, without a sample size or quantified ROI. The host's early-case-insights speed claim and mention of Harvey's agentic capabilities are not treated as Mazares's findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Mazares describes a multi-year, uneven transition, conditional on experienced people, training and reliable processes.
pts.d: Mazares characterizes adoption as an evolution occurring over many years, with AI-intensive, partly AI-enabled and non-AI review coexisting for a few years despite accelerating uptake. His junior-associate and billing predictions answer a question framed around the next three to five years; he does not independently give a more precise deadline. He conditions the benefits on legal grounding, technology expertise and continued learning, and explicitly notes that he is not a lawyer. Moore's observations concern current advisory demand, including renewals of tools purchased a year to eighteen months earlier.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes principally affect litigation-support providers, document reviewers, junior associates, law firms and corporate legal buyers.
pts.d: For service providers and their staff, Mazares anticipates higher productivity, more sophisticated advisory work and changing revenue sources. Review staffing varies by project and adoption level. Junior associates may become fewer but more productive, while needing alternatives to the learning previously gained from document review; senior partners and corporate clients may learn AI applications from juniors. Clients are expected to resist paying for hours that technology makes unnecessary while continuing to value expert support. Moore's affected groups are law-firm management, attorneys and legal departments assessing readiness and expensive subscription commitments. Neither speaker makes a specific access-to-justice claim.
